Semi Truck Tire Size Guide: Reading the Sidewall

Published 2026-03-10 · Updated 2026-07-22 · Xpress Tire Center

Quick answer

A semi truck tire size like 295/75R22.5 reads as section width 295 millimeters, aspect ratio 75 percent of that width for sidewall height, R for radial construction, and 22.5 inch wheel diameter. Sizes written as 11R22.5 use the older numeric format where 11 is section width in inches. The most common North American commercial sizes are 11R22.5, 295/75R22.5, 11R24.5 and 285/75R24.5.

Two formats, one meaning

Commercial truck tires are written two ways and both are still in daily use. The numeric format, 11R22.5, gives section width in inches followed by construction and rim diameter. The metric format, 295/75R22.5, gives section width in millimeters, then the aspect ratio, then construction and rim diameter. They are not interchangeable even when they look close: 11R22.5 and 295/75R22.5 have similar widths but different overall diameters and load characteristics.

SizeTypical positionCommon use
11R22.5Steer, drive, trailerThe default North American Class 8 size
295/75R22.5Steer, drive, trailerLow-profile alternative, better fuel economy
11R24.5Steer, drive, trailerTaller, more tread volume, older-spec tractors
285/75R24.5Steer, drive, trailerLow-profile 24.5, common on late-model sleepers
245/70R19.5All positionsMedium duty, box trucks, buses, RVs
225/70R19.5All positionsLight medium duty, delivery
385/65R22.5Steer, lift axleWide-base steer, heavy front loads
445/50R22.5TrailerSuper single wide-base trailer position

Load range and ply rating

Load range letters replaced the old ply rating but the industry still uses both. Load range G is roughly a 14-ply rating, H is 16-ply, and J is 18-ply. Load range determines how much weight a tire can legally carry at a given inflation pressure, which is why you cannot solve an overload problem by adding air beyond the sidewall maximum. Match the load range to the axle rating, not to what was on the truck when you bought it.

Position matters more than brand

  • Steer tires use a rib tread for stability and even wear, and carry the highest safety consequence. Do not run a used or questionable casing on the steer axle.
  • Drive tires use a lug or block tread for traction. This is where retreads make the most economic sense on a regional fleet.
  • Trailer tires use a shallow rib designed for free rolling, low heat and scrub resistance. Running drive tires on a trailer wastes money.
  • All-position tires exist and are a compromise. They are useful for mixed fleets that cannot inventory three tread designs.

Never mix radial and bias-ply tires on the same axle, and never mix sizes across a dual set. A diameter mismatch of even a quarter inch makes the taller tire carry a disproportionate share of the load and fail early.

What Southwest Florida duty does to tire choice

Regional Southwest Florida operation is hot, wet and heavy on stop-and-go. Heat resistance and wet traction matter more here than the last percentage point of rolling resistance. Fleets running Lee and Collier county delivery routes generally do better with a durable regional-duty tread than with a long-haul fuel-efficiency tread that will be scrubbed off by curbing and turning long before its rolling resistance advantage pays back.

This guide is written by the Xpress Tire Center team in Lehigh Acres, FL, based on real service calls on I-75 and in Lee and Collier county yards.
